name: El Presidio Real de San Francisco
summary: Founded 17 Sep 1776 by José Joaquín Moraga. A 1792 inventory found just one 3-pounder brass cannon; guns were concentrated at the Castillo, not the quadrangle.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I; NPS Golden Gate NRA
notes: Vancouver (1792) saw a brass 3-pdr lashed to a log at Fort Point and one on a rotten carriage here.

name: Provisional earthwork, Punta del Cantil Blanco
summary: Six mounted guns on a barbette platform Vancouver saw natives erecting in 1793, on Anza's 1776 cross site — superseded that August by the permanent Castillo.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I

name: Castillo de San Joaquín
summary: The flagship Spanish work, on the Fort Point bluff. Armed 1794 with eleven brass 9-pounders landed from the Aránzazu; rebuilt to a horseshoe c.1815; embrasures for 16 guns. Built by mission Native laborers. ⭐ The SF presidio company's monthly artillery relaciones give the post-rebuild armament: by 1 Apr 1816 the battery mounted 3 iron 24-pdrs, 1 iron 12-pdr (+1 burst), and 8 bronze half-culverins (8-pdr), with 2 bronze pedreros at the presidio; three iron 8-pdrs were added by May 1817 (a dozen+ serviceable guns at its Spanish-era peak). A standing 2-man 'vigía en la costa' coastal watch appears by Jan 1820 (post-Bouchard); the fort guard was 1 corporal + 4 soldiers. ⭐ The 1 Feb 1820 estado records a major post-Bouchard reconfiguration: a new iron 32-pounder, the bronze half-culverins cut from 8 to 6, three iron 4-pounders redistributed to Mission Santa Clara, and a second (new) royal flag. Into the Mexican era, the 7 Jan 1837 San Francisco artillery-park inventory (Comandante General M. G. Vallejo handing the parque to Capt. Francisco Sánchez) lists iron cannon of 24/12/8/4-lb and bronze of 10/8/2½-lb with garrison gun-carriages; by 1839 the SF, Sonoma, Monterey and Santa Bárbara detachments each held only small ordnance stocks and chronically short cartridges.
result: Demolished 1853 — cliff cut down for Fort Point
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I; Thompson, Seacoast Fortifications SF Harbor (HRS 1979) | Vallejo Documentos, BANC MSS C-B 15 (SF presidio artillery relación, 1 Apr 1816); C-B 16 (monthly relaciones 1817; estado 1 Feb 1820, the 32-pdr reconfiguration); C-B 24 (SF artillery-park inventory, 7 Jan 1837, Vallejo→Sánchez); C-B 25 (1839 presidio detachment ordnance states)
notes: Six 17th-c. Peruvian bronze cannon survive on the Presidio. Bancroft V: Frémont spiked four guns, 1 July 1846 (not five, per some sources).

name: Batería de San José / de Yerba Buena
summary: Built under Gov. Borica on Point San José (Black Point) to cover the Yerba Buena anchorage — brushwood fascines, eight embrasures, five bronze 8-pounders sent over from the Castillo. No permanent garrison.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (Prov. St. Pap. xvi.55, xvii.148–9)
notes: Second-oldest Spanish battery on the bay; derelict by 1806.

name: Castillo de San Joaquín (Mexican era)
summary: Inherited and left to decay by Mexico. An 1843 sketch shows a horseshoe adobe of 16 embrasures with only three obsolete guns and two good bronze pieces; by 1835 essentially one artilleryman.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. V

name: Presidio of San Francisco (Mexican era)
summary: Garrison shrank to 15–20 men (1824–25) and was largely relocated to El Cuartel de Sonoma (1835, Vallejo); by the 1840s the presidio was 'entirely dismantled.'
sources: Bancroft, History of California; NPS

name: Batería de Yerba Buena (Mexican era)
summary: Already ruinous 'Black Point' under Mexico; no documented refurbishment.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I

name: Fort Point (Fort Winfield Scott)
summary: Brick-and-granite casemated fort, four tiers, designed for 126 guns — the only Third System fort west of the Mississippi. Held 40 ten-inch Rodmans in its casemates by 1867.
result: Preserved — Fort Point National Historic Site (NPS)
sources: NPS Fort Point NHS; Martini, Fort Point (2016); Thompson HRS 1979
notes: Never fired a shot in anger; the Golden Gate Bridge arch was redesigned to span it.

name: Fort Alcatraz
summary: Barbette fortress with a three-story citadel — by 1863 eight batteries (South, North, West, Three-Gun, and officer-named emplacements Halleck, Rosecrans, Mansfield, Tower, McPherson, Prime) ringing the island with ~100 guns.
result: GGNRA/NPS — works buried under the later prison
sources: Martini, Fortress Alcatraz (1991); Thompson HRS 1979
notes: The most heavily armed post in the harbor; became a military prison from 1907.

name: Black Point Battery (Point San José / Fort Mason)
summary: Civil War emergency battery on the old Spanish site: West Battery six 10-inch Rodmans, East Battery six 42-pounder banded rifles.
sources: NPS Golden Gate NRA; Calif. State Military Museum
notes: Built amid fear of Confederate raiders (CSS Shenandoah).

name: Point Stuart Battery (Angel Island, Civil War)
summary: Earthwork: one 10-inch Columbiad and three 32-pounders.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum (militarymuseum.org)

name: Point Knox Battery (Angel Island, Civil War)
summary: Earthwork: seven 32-pounders, one 8-inch and two 10-inch Rodmans. Site later reused by Endicott Battery Ledyard.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum (militarymuseum.org)

name: Point Blunt Battery (Angel Island, Civil War)
summary: Earthwork of about seven smoothbores; abandoned 1866. Site later the Nike SF-91 launch area.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum (militarymuseum.org)
notes: ⚠ Exact calibers unverified — HRS pp. 57–59 to firm.

name: Water Battery (Angel Island, Civil War)
summary: Planned shoreline battery near Camp Reynolds — never completed.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum (militarymuseum.org)

name: Ridge Battery (Lime Point)
summary: Four 15-inch Rodman smoothbores on the Lime Point ridge. Battery Spencer was later built into it.
sources: FortWiki; NPS Lime Point

name: Cliff Battery (Lime Point)
summary: Two smoothbores planned; never armed; demolished 1898 to build Battery Spencer.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum; NPS

name: Gravelly Beach Battery (1870s)
summary: Water battery west of Lime Point; one 15-inch Rodman on a wooden platform — the only gun ever mounted in the 1870s Lime Point complex.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum; NPS

name: Battery Cavallo
summary: Point Cavallo earthwork; planned as a 13-gun water battery (including giant 20-inch Rodmans, never emplaced); as armed c.1900, three 8-inch converted-Rodman rifles.
sources: FortWiki; Calif. State Military Museum

name: Battery East (Presidio)

name: Battery West (Presidio)

result: Earthen wall and a magazine survive (NPS)

name: Lime Point casemate fort (endorsed, never built)
summary: The intended Marin-shore twin to Fort Point, for a crossfire across the Gate. Cliffs were blasted for a sea-level shelf in 1868–69, then abandoned when masonry was judged obsolete.
sources: NPS Lime Point; Calif. State Military Museum

name: Battery Spencer

sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979

name: Battery Duncan

name: Battery Kirby

name: Battery Orlando Wagner (Fort Baker)
summary: Two 5-inch M1897 rapid-fire guns on balanced-pillar carriages, Fort Baker; disarmed 1917.
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Yates

name: Battery Mendell

name: Battery Smith

name: Battery O'Rorke

name: Battery Godfrey

name: Battery Saffold

name: Battery Lancaster
summary: Three 12-inch guns on disappearing carriages, Fort Scott; impaired by construction of the Golden Gate Bridge.

name: Battery Marcus Miller

name: Battery Crosby
summary: Two 6-inch M1897 guns on disappearing carriages, on the bluff above Baker Beach, to protect the Golden Gate minefields.

name: Battery William McKinnon
summary: Eight 12-inch mortars — the other half of the 'McKinnon-Stotsenburg' work.

name: Battery Boutelle
summary: Three 5-inch M1897 guns on balanced-pillar carriages, Fort Scott; disarmed 1917.
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Sherwood
summary: Two 5-inch M1900 guns on pedestal mounts in the national-cemetery area, Fort Scott — the only battery of its type in the SF Endicott defenses.

name: Battery Slaughter
summary: Three 8-inch M1888 guns on disappearing carriages, Fort Scott; disarmed 1917.

summary: Two 3-inch (15-pounder) M1898 guns on masking-parapet carriages, Fort Scott.

name: Battery Blaney
summary: Four 3-inch M1898 guns on masking-parapet carriages, Fort Scott; dismounted 1920.

name: Dynamite Battery
summary: Three 15-inch pneumatic dynamite guns — unique on the Pacific Coast (only one other in the U.S., at Sandy Hook). Reused in WWII as the Harbor Defense Command Post.

name: Battery Chamberlin

name: Battery Livingston
summary: Eight 12-inch mortars (originally 16, split 1906), Fort Miley.
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Springer
summary: Eight 12-inch mortars — the other half of the Livingston mortar block, Fort Miley.
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Chester
summary: Three 12-inch guns (two on disappearing carriages, one barbette), Fort Miley.
sources: FortWiki

summary: Two 5-inch M1900 guns (from Battery Ledyard, Angel Island), Fort Miley.
result: DEMOLISHED — destroyed by VA Hospital expansion
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Burnham (Fort Mason)
summary: One 8-inch gun on a disappearing carriage atop Point San José, above the Civil War Batteries East and West; short-lived — field of fire blocked by the city.
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Drew (Angel Island)
summary: One 8-inch gun on a barbette carriage on Martar Hill — Angel Island's first Endicott battery, twin of Battery Duncan.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 428

name: Battery Ledyard (Angel Island)
summary: Two 5-inch M1900 guns on pedestal mounts, on the old Point Knox site; twin of Battery Sherwood. Guns went to Battery Call in 1915.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 429
notes: ⚠ Disarm date 1915 (FortWiki) vs 1920 (militarymuseum).

name: Battery Wallace (Angel Island)
summary: One 8-inch gun on a disappearing carriage — the only disappearing gun on the island; similar to Battery Burnham, Fort Mason.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 428
notes: Distinct from the larger Battery Wallace at Fort Barry.

name: Battery Wallace (Fort Barry)
summary: Two 12-inch M1895 guns on long-range barbette carriages (360°), casemated in 1942–43 — Fort Barry's heaviest surviving long-range battery.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979

name: Battery Construction No. 129 (Fort Barry)
summary: Designed for two 16-inch navy guns on Diablo Ridge, over 800 ft — 'one of the highest seacoast batteries in the world.' Tubes arrived but carriages were never delivered; never armed. Would have been the harbor's third 16-inch battery.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 445
notes: On Hawk Hill / Diablo Ridge (~820 ft), Fort Barry — verified via FortWiki (the earlier 'inland error' flag was itself wrong; Hawk Hill really is here). The Nike SF-87 control area later sat on this hill.

name: Battery Townsley
summary: Two 16-inch guns on casemated carriages on Wolf Ridge, Fort Cronkhite — the largest guns ever emplaced at the Golden Gate; first fired 1 July 1940, the first 16-inch round on the U.S. Pacific coast.
result: Extant casemated battery, partly restored — display 16-inch gun since 2012
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979; Chin, Artillery at the Golden Gate (1994)

name: Anti-Aircraft Battery No. 1 (Wolf Ridge)
summary: Three-inch anti-aircraft guns protecting Battery Townsley, with its own powerhouse and magazine.
result: Concrete emplacements survive on Wolf Ridge
sources: Calif. State Military Museum
notes: ⚠ Gun count: militarymuseum 3, FortWiki 2.

name: Battery Kirby Beach (Gravelly Beach 3-inch)
summary: Two 3-inch guns (from Battery Yates), Fort Baker shoreline; octagonal gun blocks; guns later moved to Fort Point.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 446

name: Battery Gravelly (AMTB, Fort Baker)
summary: Two 90 mm guns on fixed mounts and two on mobile mounts, Gravelly (Kirby) Beach; circular gun blocks — the permanent north-shore anti-motor-torpedo-boat battery.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 446

name: Battery Bonita (AMTB, Fort Barry)
summary: Two 37 mm automatic weapons (1943) replaced by two 40 mm (1944), at Point Bonita.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 446

name: Cavallo Battery (AMTB, WWII)
summary: Two 37 mm (1943) then 40 mm (1944) automatic weapons — one at the tip of Point Cavallo, one on the Fort Baker mine wharf.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 446

name: Battery Gate (Fort Point)
summary: Two 3-inch guns (from Battery Yates) mounted on the barbette tier of the old masonry fort.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 447
notes: A distinct battery from Battery Point — together they were the four 3-inch guns on the Fort Point barbette tier.

name: Battery Point (Fort Point)
summary: Two 3-inch guns (from Battery Yates), first at Gravelly Beach, later moved to the Fort Point barbette tier.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 447

name: Battery Baker (AMTB, Bakers Beach)
summary: Two 90 mm guns on fixed mounts and two on mobile mounts, in front of the mine casemate at Bakers Beach; guarded the minefield and harbor entrance.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 447
notes: A real WWII battery — the 'no Battery Baker' note applies only to the Endicott era.

name: Battery Scott (AMTB)
summary: Two 40 mm guns — one at Fort Point, one at Bakers Beach; retained in the 1945 planning supplement.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 447

name: Battery Lobos (Fort Miley)
summary: Two 6-inch navy guns on pedestal mounts, emplaced on Point Lobos.
result: Pad 1 partly exposed below the USS San Francisco Memorial
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 448

name: Battery Construction No. 243 (Fort Miley)
summary: Two 6-inch guns on shielded barbette carriages — the last gun battery armed at San Francisco (guns finally mounted in 1948).
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 448

name: Battery Land (AMTB, Lands End)
summary: Two 90 mm guns on fixed mounts and two on mobile mounts, at Lands End north of Fort Miley.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 448

name: Battery Buck (AMTB, Fort Miley)
summary: Two 37 mm automatic weapons, later replaced by 40 mm, in the Fort Miley / Lands End vicinity.
sources: Thompson HRS 1979 p. 448

name: Battery Davis (Fort Funston)
summary: Two 16-inch navy guns in earth-covered concrete casemates — the first casemated 16-inch battery in the United States and the engineering prototype for the whole WWII casemated program. Tubes were originally forged for the cancelled battlecruiser USS Saratoga.
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979; Chin (1994)

name: Battery Howe (Fort Funston)
summary: Four 12-inch mortars (from Stotsenburg-McKinnon), in an unusual straight-line pit layout.
sources: FortWiki; Calif. State Military Museum
notes: Distinct from Fort Scott's Battery Howe.

name: Battery Bruff (Fort Funston)
summary: Two 5-inch M1900 guns — the shortest-lived battery in the SF defenses, obsolete about six months after transfer.
sources: FortWiki
notes: A separate battery from Battery Bluff, not a spelling variant.

name: Battery Bluff (Fort Funston)
summary: Four mobile 155 mm guns on Panama mounts — the only Panama mounts in San Francisco. The original clifftop site eroded, forcing a move south; original mounts remain in the surf.
result: Panama mounts visible at the cliff base (GGNRA)
sources: FortWiki; Thompson HRS 1979 p. 449
notes: 'Bluff' is a descriptive name (the ocean bluff), not an officer namesake.

name: Battery AA5 (Fort Funston)
summary: Three 3-inch M1917 guns on fixed anti-aircraft mounts — the only named fixed AA battery at Funston.
result: Magazine, power room, and three gun blocks extant (GGNRA)
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Construction No. 244 (Milagra Ridge)
summary: Two 6-inch guns on shielded barbette carriages atop Milagra Ridge, Pacifica.
sources: FortWiki

name: Battery Construction No. 130 (Milagra, unbuilt)
summary: Planned two 16-inch casemated battery at Milagra Ridge — cancelled during the war, never started.
sources: FortWiki (Milagra Ridge Military Reservation)

name: Angel Island AMTB batteries (Blunt / Knox / Cove)
summary: Programmed anti-motor-torpedo-boat batteries at Points Blunt, Knox, and Ione (Cove) — 90 mm and 40 mm — plus four mobile 90 mm AA guns sited at the Endicott emplacements.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum
notes: Point Blunt later overbuilt by the Nike SF-91 site.

name: U.S. Navy Net Depot, Tiburon
summary: Assembled and deployed the roughly 7-mile, 6,000-ton anti-submarine steel net strung across the Golden Gate (terminals at Sausalito/Lime Point and Fort Point) — the physical barrier complementing the minefields.
result: Now SF State's Estuary & Ocean Science Center
sources: NPS; U.S. Navy Net Depot Tiburon (Wikipedia)

name: Yerba Buena Island Torpedo (Mine) Assembly Building
summary: Stored and assembled the controlled submarine mines for the bay defense. Army gun batteries planned for the island (1861, 1868) were never built.
result: Island now Navy/Coast Guard and City of SF
sources: FortWiki (Camp Yerba Buena Island)

name: Nike SF-08/09 — San Pablo Ridge (Tilden)
summary: A double Nike Ajax site (09 launch, 08 control) in the Berkeley hills, the two batteries covering each other's dead zones.
sources: Ed Thelen Nike database; Calif. State Military Museum

name: Nike SF-25 — Rocky Ridge (San Ramon)
summary: A short-lived Nike Ajax site in the Las Trampas hills — one of the briefest in the Bay Area.
sources: Ed Thelen Nike database; San Ramon Valley Historical Society

name: Nike SF-31 — Lake Chabot / Castro Valley
summary: Nike Ajax upgraded to nuclear-capable Hercules; one of the last three Bay-area sites deactivated (March 1974).
result: Demolished — East Bay Regional Park District

name: Nike SF-37 — Coyote Hills (Fremont)
summary: A Nike Ajax site on the southeast bay shore.

name: Benicia Arsenal — Clock Tower Fortress
summary: The fortified sandstone bastion of the Benicia Arsenal on Army Point, built 1859 with gun ports and rifle slits covering the Carquinez Strait and Suisun Bay — called the first stone fortress in the far West. Originally two towers; rebuilt with one after an 1912 powder explosion.
sources: HMDB (Benicia Clock Tower); Benicia Arsenal Historic District

name: Anti-Aircraft Battery No. 2 (Fort Barry)
summary: Three 3-inch M1917 anti-aircraft guns at Fort Barry (shown on the WWII harbor-defense maps). Exact placement not recorded in the sources.
sources: Calif. State Military Museum; northamericanforts.com

name: Mare Island AA defenses (WWII)
summary: Mare Island Navy Yard was defended in WWII by MOBILE 90 mm AA guns and .50-cal machine guns (211th Coast Artillery, on station a week after Pearl Harbor) plus barrage balloons (309th CA Balloon Bn), in positions spread across the south end, Hwy 37, and North Vallejo. The yard never had a FIXED coastal-defense gun battery — San Pablo Bay was screened by the Golden Gate forts ~20 mi downstream.
result: ⚠ Mobile AA only — no fixed seacoast battery; air-raid siren tower & shelter booths survive
sources: North American Forts (ca-central); Calif. State Military Museum (Mare Island / HDSF)
notes: Civil War: a garrison (soldiers on USS Independence, then Marines), no mounted gun battery. Endicott era: explicitly excluded from the Harbor Defenses of San Francisco. FortWiki lists Mare Island as a Navy yard, not a coast-defense fort. Position approximate (south-end AA site).

name: Carquinez AMTB battery (Crockett / Valona Hill)

sources: Calif. State Military Museum; northamericanforts.com

name: Eliza's Activo at Bodega — Spain's Last Pacific Exploration
summary: Eliza arrives in Activo after near-starvation NW Coast voyage. Spain's last Pacific exploration. The exhausted vessel barely makes it to Bodega — the empire's reach is collapsing.
result: Last Spanish Pacific exploration — barely survived

name: Golden Gate Crossing — Borrowed Launches
summary: 32 horses ferried across the Golden Gate using launches borrowed from visiting San Blas frigates Princesa and Aranzazu. Spain cannot cross its own bay without foreign ships.

name: Viceroy Orders Bodega — "Whether or Not English Are There"

name: English at Bodega "con los cañones en tierra"

name: Zúñiga Shows Bodega Plans to British — No Concealment
summary: San Diego commandant Zúñiga freely shows Bodega harbor plans to British officers. No concealment at all — contradicts the tight security at SF. The policy was inconsistent.
result: Concealment policy fails at San Diego
sources: Menzies 1924:335.

name: RAC Fur-Collecting Begins at Bodega
summary: 130 Aleut hunters aboard Kodiak. First Russian representative: Tarakanov. 40+ Russians + 150 Indians by 1809 (Argüello report). Moraga protests — ignored.
result: Permanent Russian presence established — Spain protests but cannot act
sources: Milliken 2009:22–25; C-A 12.

name: 130 Bidarkas in San Francisco Bay
summary: 130 Aleut bidarkas (kayaks) hunting sea otter inside San Francisco Bay. The Russians are inside Spain's premier port and Spain cannot stop them.
result: Russian hunting inside the Bay — sovereignty violated
sources: C-A 12 (Prov. St. Pap. XIX).

name: Farallon Islands — Russian Sealing Station
summary: Russian sealing station on the Farallones — 18 miles off the coast of San Francisco. Aleut hunters camped seasonally. Spain/Mexico never contested it.
result: Russian territory visible from SF — unchallenged
sources: Bancroft II; Fort Ross sources.

name: Hagemeister Treaty with Kashaya Pomo
summary: Russia negotiates land cession with Kashaya Pomo chiefs — not Spanish authorities. "Allies of Russia" medals distributed 1819. Russians treat indigenous peoples as sovereign landowners because, north of the Bay, they are.
result: Russia treats Pomo as sovereign — Spain does not exist here
sources: hagemeister-pomo-treaty-1817; AVPRI documents.

name: Kuskov's RAC Letters to the SF Commandant
summary: Ivan Kuskov, RAC commercial councillor at Ross, writes directly to the SF commandant "in the name of the Honorable Russian-American Company under special protection of His Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias," sending agent Slobodchikov to settle accounts and pressing for the return of captured Kodiak Aleuts.
result: Ross corresponds with SF as one sovereign to another

name: Spanish Missions Supply Kuskov at Fort Ross
summary: The Spanish missions supplying Kuskov's Russian colony — Spain's own establishments provisioning the foreign outpost on the ground it claimed. The open coast as routine economic fact, running in Spain's disfavor.
result: Spain provisions the colony it was ordered to uproot

name: Fort Ross Abandonment Resolved
summary: The RAC Main Board resolves to abandon Ross and "sell or barter for wheat to the inhabitants of San Francisco." The otter gone, Ross is liquidated — the economic close of the arc that opened with the resource.
result: Russia leaves — Ross sold to Sutter, a promoter of the US invasion
sources: Fort Ross AVPRI, 1841 abandonment resolution (via Gibson & Istomin).

name: RAC Parlamentario — Podushkin on the Chirikoff at Monterey
summary: Baranov, from Novo-Arkhangelsk, protests the "insults to the Russian Flag and the capture and keeping in cruel bondage of Russians… in the waters and the coasts of California," invokes the 1812 treaty, and sends Lt. Podushkin as a parlamentario aboard the Chirikoff to Monterey. Russia negotiating as a commercial sovereign on Spain's claimed coast.
result: Russia treats with Spain as an equal power on the California coast
sources: C-A 13 Docs 263–264 (Podushkin's request, 22 Apr 1817; Baranov's protest, 2 Feb 1817). Formerly cited as survey entry 20.

name: Yanovsky's RAC Trade Overture
summary: RAC chief manager Semyon Yanovsky proposes a joint, equal-shares otter-hunt and open commerce (via Khlebnikov and the Madrid embassy; the Ilmena to supply Ross). Solá replies he cannot grant otter-hunting — only the Viceroy can. The third volume of one continuous Russo-Spanish negotiation.
result: Russia again negotiates as a commercial sovereign — Spain defers to Mexico City
sources: C-A 55 Docs 323–324 (Yanovsky / Solá, ~1820).

name: The Suvorov at SF + the RAC Proclamation to California
summary: The RAC ship Suvorov (Lazarev) calls at San Francisco carrying a formal RAC directors' overture "to the noble and honoured Spanish inhabitants of California," invoking Russo-Spanish friendship, the 1812 treaty, and Rezanov's 1806 visit — the institutional Russian demand for the California provision trade, arriving by ship.
result: The RAC's formal trade-opening request, delivered to SF
sources: C-A 12 C478 + C479 (Suvorov 1815; passport-proclamation St. Petersburg, 12 Jul 1811).

name: Rezanov Arrives on Juno
summary: Nikolai Rezanov — Imperial Chamberlain, RAC shareholder, diplomat. Arrives at SF. Concepción Argüello courtship. Intelligence gathering on Spanish defenses. First Russian official at SF.
sources: Bancroft II; Gibson & Istomin 2014.

name: Coast Miwok Intelligence to Sal
summary: Coast Miwok informant tells Commandant Sal two ships at Bodega — soldiers "dressed like ours turned inside out." Earliest warning of foreign presence, 3 weeks before diplomatic intelligence through official channels.
result: Indigenous networks faster than imperial intelligence

name: Coast Miwok Deceive Goycoechea
summary: Coast Miwok tell Goycoechea the eastern shores are "impassable" — he takes the harder western route via Marin headlands. Later admitted he was "deceived." Information control: indigenous peoples directing Spanish military movements.

name: Coast Miwok Calibrated Diplomacy at Bodega

result: Military capability held in reserve — diplomacy chosen

summary: Coast Miwok calling "Amico," speaking Spanish, pointing up lagoon repeating "Spaniard." Bilingual intermediaries positioning between British and Spanish empires. They know both powers and broker between them.
sources: Menzies 1924:302.

name: Colony Ross (Russian benchmark)

Either figure matches or exceeds the serviceable artillery of the entire San Francisco defense in the same decade.

name: Presidio of San Francisco

name: Fort San Joaquín (Castillo de SF)
summary: 1794. Battery guarding the Golden Gate narrows. 1 cannon (burst 1792), 8 by 1793, 6 functional by 1820. Unmanned by 1800.

name: Mission San Rafael
summary: 1817. Anti-Russian buffer. 83 days after Hagemeister treaty. Founded without a boat.

name: Bodega y Quadra discovers and charts the port
summary: The schooner Sonora under Bodega y Quadra and pilot Francisco Mourelle charts the port on the return leg of the 1775 voyage. Their manuscript plano, with keyed points and soundings, is the founding document of the Spanish claim. The chart is in this site's gallery.
sources: Plano del Puerto del Capitan Bodega (LOC, gallery item loc-bq05); resurveyed 1793 (Cartas esfericas sheet 8)

name: The 1793 occupation attempt fails
summary: The year Spain finally moved to occupy Bodega: Matute's establishment attempt, mounted amid the Nootka crisis, was abandoned. The port Spain had claimed in 1775 stayed empty, and the re-survey of the same year became its monument. The full argument is the subject of the companion article.
result: Spain never occupied the port it discovered
sources: C-A 55 (Matute dossier); the 1793 re-survey, Cartas esfericas sheet 8 (gallery)
notes: Deliberately summary-level here; the article carries the argument and the full citations.

name: The 1811 Aleut otter fleet in San Francisco Bay

name: Vallejo's reconnaissance of Ross (informe reservado)

name: Ross sold to Sutter; the Russians withdraw
summary: The Russian-American Company sells the Ross establishment to John Sutter and withdraws from California, ending the colony the Spanish had watched for thirty years without ever dislodging.

summary: Returns after 10 days. Report confirms Russian presence and fur-hunting operations at Bodega.
