sources: Standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal., IV); cf. Leg. Rec. (C-A 61) Doc 19

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: 1797. Moraga 1806 departure; Viader 1810 Aug return.

name: Mission San Fernando
summary: 1797. Moraga 1806 arrival.

name: Mission San José
summary: 1797. Viader/Moraga 1810 departure point.

name: Mission Santa Clara
summary: 1777. Viader 1810 Oct return.

name: Mission San Miguel
summary: 1797. Moraga 1807 stop.

name: Monterey Presidio
summary: Moraga 1807 departure.

name: Mission San Rafael
summary: 1817. First establishment north of SF Bay. Site selected by Moraga. Founded 83 days after Hagemeister-Pomo treaty.

name: Fort Ross
summary: 1812. Russian-American Company. Kuskov. 95 Russians + ~80 Aleut hunters. Moraga visited 1812, 1813, 1814.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: 1776. Founded by José Joaquín Moraga (Gabriel's father). Gabriel served here as Alférez 1806–1818.

name: Monterey
summary: Departure. 25 cavalry under Alférez Gabriel Moraga. Sgt. Miguel Espinosa. 8 horses each.

name: Mission San Miguel
summary: 'We went from Monterey to San Miguel Mission.'

name: Buena Vista Lake
summary: 'From there to the Laguna we called Buena Vista in one day and a half.' Went after runaway neophytes — 'did not get any.'
sources: Cook note 46: 'This expedition of 1807 is otherwise unrecorded.'

name: Mountains — Salinas de Cortéz
summary: 'We went away into the Snowy Mountains.' Indians stole half the horses and killed two men. 'Portezuelo' with great quantities of nitre.
sources: Cook note 47: possibly entrance to Gorge of Kern R., E of Bakersfield

name: San Joaquin River (crossings)
summary: 'We crossed the San Joaquin River several times and everywhere there was Indians.'

name: Mission San José
summary: 'The Captain made up his mind to go back by the way of San Jose Mission where we arrived in good order.'

name: Mission San José
summary: Aug 15, 1810. Departed 5:30pm with Lt. Moraga, Cadet Estrada, 1 corporal, 3 soldiers, 4 neophytes.

name: Valley of San José — Pool
summary: Aug 15. 6 leagues N. 'Good water. So near and so well known to everyone.'

name: Walnut Creek
summary: Aug 16 (lunch). 6 leagues N. 'Good water but runs in very small amount.' Killed 2 bears and a deer.
sources: Cook note 1: route via Sunol, Dublin, Walnut Creek

name: End of Walnut Creek — Estuaries
summary: Aug 16. 6 more leagues N. 'Beginning of some estuaries on the NE side of a fine plain.' Big walnut trees.

name: San Joaquin R. / Tulpunes — Antioch
summary: Aug 18. 7 leagues E. 'Quarter-league wide, apparently very deep, reached by tides.' Large oak forest. Tulpunes not seen.
sources: Cook note 2: at or near Antioch. Julpunes oak forest to Brentwood.

name: Oak Forest — Oakley
summary: Aug 18. 2 more leagues E. Good country, no water except the river.
sources: Cook note 2: halt near Oakley

name: Pescadero / Cholvones — Bethany
summary: Aug 19. 10 leagues SE. Lake in oak grove. Interpreter met heathen Guanats. 'Christian fugitives from San Jose on opposite shore.'
sources: Cook note 3: Bethany. Lakes vanished.

name: Tomchom Village
summary: Aug 20. 3 leagues SSE. 'No wild Indian showed himself.'
sources: Cook note 4: north of Tracy

name: Cuyens Village
summary: Aug 20. 2½ leagues further. Chief Cuyens. 15 Indians brought fish. 4 stayed the night.
sources: Cook note 4: left bank, 3 mi above highway bridge

name: Maijem Village
summary: Aug 21. 2½–3 leagues. Dry stream bed. Indians came 'with great trepidation' then disappeared.
sources: Cook note 5: ~2 mi NNE of Vernalis

name: Opposite Bozenats Village
summary: Aug 21. 2 leagues. Indians on far bank 'refused to come near, yelled with much vigor.'
sources: Cook note 6: right bank, E of Vernalis

name: SKIRMISH — Tationes / Apaglamenes
summary: Aug 22. 2 leagues + 1 league. 30 armed heathen on opposite bank. Then Tationes village. Apaglamenes and Tationes attacked — 'painted, bedecked with feathers.' 12 shots fired. One Indian hit.
sources: Cook note 7: ~2 mi SE of Grayson

name: Lakes near Willow Grove
summary: Aug 22 afternoon. 3 leagues. 'Neither firewood nor good land.'
sources: Cook note 8: probably E of Patterson

name: Creek — Orestimba
summary: Aug 23. 3½ leagues. 'Great heat forced us to jump in for a swim.'
sources: Cook note 9: Orestimba Cr., E of Crows Landing

name: Pond — NE of Gustine
summary: Aug 23. 4 leagues. 'No wood or brush to cook supper or even make chocolate.'
sources: Cook note 10: 3–4 mi NE of Gustine. Southernmost point.

name: San Luis Gonzaga
summary: Aug 24. Turned back W! 10 leagues. Explored — 'no more water than a few pools.' Not suitable for mission.

name: Ausaymas Creek
summary: Aug 26. SW over mountains. 'Caught forty fish including six trout.' Already the plain of San Juan Bautista.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Aug 27. 5 leagues SW. 'With a good breakfast we brought the expedition to an end.' Signed Fr. José Viader, Aug 28, 1810.

name: Mission San José
summary: Oct 19, 1810. Left ~2pm with Lt. Moraga, 23 soldiers, ~50 armed Christian Indians.

name: Valley of San José
summary: Oct 19. 6 leagues NE. Willow grove with good water.

name: Pescadero / Cholvones — Bethany
summary: Oct 20. 9 leagues ENE. 'Arrived very late so as not to be seen or heard. Placed our people in position to attack a dance.'
sources: Cook note 11: Mission San José to Bethany = ~32 mi

name: Bolbones Villages — Old River
summary: Oct 21. 'Before dawn we assaulted a village.' Captured 15 San Jose Christians, 18 heathen men, 51 women. Women released — 'went away very happy.' Two prisoners escaped.
sources: Cook note 12: two villages on Old River / Union I.

name: Jusmites
summary: Oct 22. 2½ leagues SE along river. 'Oak groves, willow thickets, ponds.'
sources: Cook note 14

name: Tugites
summary: Oct 22. 2½ more leagues. 'All the country has wood, water in the river and lakes, but the land is low, flooded.'
sources: Cook note 14

name: Cuyens Village
summary: Oct 23. Met friendly Cuyens Indians. 'Bearing as a gift three very big, red, salmon.'

name: Mayem Village
summary: Oct 23. 4 leagues total. 'Approached us with much fear and a tendency to prevaricate.' Deny harboring Christians. Lt. threatens flogging.
sources: Cook note 14: Mayem 9 leagues from Pescadero

name: Ford Opposite Taualames
summary: Oct 23 afternoon. 2 leagues. 'Ford across the river — very bad, wide and deep.' Crossed without incident. Sent boy to village.
sources: Cook note 14–15

name: Toward Tuolumne — Blocked
summary: Oct 24. Scouted N toward Tuolumne (Dolores), 2–3 leagues away. 'On account of so many sloughs, swamps, and ponds we turned back.'

name: Past Apelamenes & Tatives
summary: Oct 24 afternoon. 6 leagues SSE. 'Passed in front of the Apelamenes and Tatives Indians, who had fought us on the former occasion.'

name: Merced River
summary: Oct 24. Reached Merced R. 'Almost swimming the horses.' Much wood — oak, cypress, cottonwood.
sources: Cook note 15

name: Crossed San Joaquin
summary: Oct 25. SW. 'Crossed several other swampy sloughs. Southward no more trees, only tules.'

name: 'Battle / Shaving Place'
summary: Oct 25. 2½ leagues downstream. 'At this point now, as previously, the soldiers shave themselves.'

name: Orestimba Creek — Apalamenes
summary: Oct 25. 1 league. 'Allies of the Tatives when they fought us.' Creek dry. 'Least bad spot — only firewood, river water, and good fish.'
sources: Cook note 9/16

name: Opposite Taualames (return)
summary: Oct 25. 2 leagues. 'Refused to come out, saying they were afraid. They guessed right for they would have been taken captive.'

name: Del Puerto Creek — Corpus Christi
summary: Oct 25. 3 leagues W. 'Spent the night without water for the horses. Had to dig a well in the sand.'
sources: Cook note 16: Del Puerto Cr.

name: El Toro
summary: Oct 26. 6 leagues W. Mountains, bad trails. Lunch stop.

name: San Guillermo
summary: Oct 26. 6 more leagues W. 'Extremely bad trail.' Pools of good water.

name: Old Village of Patenos
summary: Oct 27. 6 leagues W. Lunch stop.
sources: Cook note 16: through hills NE of Mt. Hamilton

name: Mission Santa Clara
summary: Oct 27. 5 leagues NW. 'In good condition, thanks be to God.' Signed Fr. José Viader, Oct 28, 1810.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: May 1810. Governor Arrillaga orders Moraga to pursue the Suisun, who have killed 16 Christians over 3 years. Moraga departs with 17 men.
sources: Arrillaga report, Prov. Rec. ix. 122–3 (C-A 25).

name: Overland March — East Bay Hills
summary: Route overland from the Presidio, skirting the south shore of the Bay toward the Strait. Exact route unknown but likely through modern Oakland/Richmond hills.
sources: No diary survives for this expedition.

name: Carquinez Strait Crossing
summary: Troops had no boats. Found a single small vessel. 'With great sacrifice, the Ensign embarked his troops and horses, making several crossings.' Multiple trips across the narrows.
sources: Arrillaga report. Vallejo calls it the 'Karkin-aku pass.'

name: Skirmish on Suisun Creek
summary: Initial engagement. After crossing the strait, troops fought Suisun warriors along the banks of a creek. Vallejo (via Sánchez): the Suisun chief drew the Spanish inland toward the main body of warriors. Sgt. Francisco Soto left as rear guard with horses.
sources: Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos, i. 131–5. Vallejo attributes to Sánchez (1817) but likely describes 1810.

name: Battle at Malaca's Ranchería
summary: Main engagement, May 22, 1810. Captured 18 gentiles (released — too wounded to transport). Survivors retreated into 3 tule huts. 2 corporals (Herrera, Soto) and 2 soldiers (Briones, Zúñiga) wounded. After 2 huts stormed, 3rd set on fire. Defenders burned alive rather than surrender. ~120 Suisun fighters. Chief Malaca's speech: 'It is better to die free than to live as slaves, despised by our Puy.'
sources: Bancroft II, p. 91 fn. 24. Arrillaga: Prov. Rec. ix. 122–3. Royal Order: Prov. St. Pap. xix. 314. Vallejo: MS. i. 131–5.

name: Return Crossing — Carquinez Strait
summary: Vallejo: 'At dawn they tried to ford a creek and came back over the Carquines Strait.' Return to south shore after the battle.
sources: Vallejo, Recuerdos, i. 131–5.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Moraga returns to the Presidio. Arrillaga reports to the Viceroy on June 20, 1810. Royal Order arrives Nov. 12, 1811: Moraga promoted to brevet Lieutenant of Cavalry.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: October 3, 1810. Governor orders Moraga to investigate Russian fur-hunting at Bodega Bay. 10-day reconnaissance.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, fn. 52: 'Gabriel Moraga's Diary of his Expedition to the Port of Bodega, Oct. 3, 1810, Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.' Diary survives in the Archives of California.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay from the Presidio to the Marin shore. Method uncertain — possibly native balsas or a borrowed vessel.
sources: SF Presidio had limited boat access. See boat-problem article.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Passed through future site of Mission San Rafael. Bancroft: 'The site was probably selected on the advice of Moraga, who had several times passed it on his way to and from Bodega.'
sources: Bancroft, II, p. 330.

name: Novato / Olompali Area
summary: Route north through Marin. Approximate — following the natural corridor through the Novato gap toward Petaluma Creek and the coast.
sources: Exact route not specified in diary abstract.

name: Petaluma Creek / Estuary
summary: Likely crossed or followed Petaluma Creek toward the coast. Natural route from interior Marin to Bodega Bay.
sources: Route reconstruction based on geography.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Arrived at Bodega Bay. Found an American ship and Alaskan Indians (Aleut hunters working for the Russian-American Company). 10-day reconnaissance of the area. Wrote a diary of the expedition.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: 'finds an American ship and Alaskan Indians.' Diary: Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns after 10 days. Report confirms Russian presence and fur-hunting operations at Bodega.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: July 1812. Argüello sends Moraga with 4 men to investigate construction of a small Russian fort on the Sonoma coast. Fort Ross had been dedicated Sept. 10, 1812 — but Kuskov had been building since spring.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay to the Marin shore.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Through future Mission San Rafael site. Moraga's repeated passage through here informed his later recommendation of the site.

name: Petaluma Creek Area
summary: North through Marin toward the coast. Approximate route.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Passed through or near Bodega Bay en route to Fort Ross.

name: Fort Ross
summary: Moraga identifies the Russian settlement: a brigantine-anchored base with a 150-yard-square stockade and cannon. Notes the Russians' friendly manner. Fort Ross had been dedicated by Kuskov with 95 Russians and ~80 Aleut hunters.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: '150-yard-square stockade and cannon; notes the Russians' friendly manner.'

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to SF. Report filed with Argüello.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: January 1813. Moraga drives 20 cattle and 3 horses to Fort Ross — practical diplomacy. Returns again in 1814 with Cadet Gervasio Argüello.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed bay to Marin shore with livestock.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Through future mission site, driving cattle north.

name: Bodega Bay Area
summary: Through Bodega country toward Fort Ross.

name: Fort Ross
summary: Jan. 1813: Delivered 20 cattle, 3 horses as goodwill gesture. 1814 return: accompanied by Cadet Gervasio Argüello. Wrote a report describing 40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon, glass windows in the commandant's house. Also carried official demands for Russian withdrawal.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: '40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon guarding the place, and glass windows in the commandant's house.'

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to SF Presidio.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: c. 1817. Moraga reconnoiters the site north of the Bay for a new establishment. He had passed through this area multiple times on trips to Bodega and Fort Ross since 1810.
sources: Bancroft II, p. 330: 'The site was probably selected on the advice of Moraga.'

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay to the Marin shore. SF Presidio had no proper boat from Feb. 1816 to Nov. 1818 — crossing method uncertain. Possibly native tule balsas.
sources: See boat-problem article. Vallejo mentions 'a small boat belonging to the San Francisco presidio.'

name: Mission San Rafael Site
summary: Moraga selects this site — 5 leagues north of the Presidio, on the other side of the Bay. Warmer climate, near homeland of many SF neophytes. Mission founded Dec. 14, 1817 under Fr. Luis Gil y Taboada, escorted by Cpl. José Herrera (wounded at Suisun 1810, promoted to Sgt.). Vallejo says the Suisun victory led directly to the decision to found the mission.
sources: Solá letter: Prov. Rec. ix. 583–604 (C-A 25). Founded 83 days after Hagemeister-Pomo treaty.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to the Presidio with his recommendation. Governor Solá approves the plan in consultation with Prefect Sarría.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: The northernmost presidio, founded 1776, responsible for the whole contested frontier facing Bodega and Ross. Its company ran about 30 to 56 men for most of the Spanish period and never surged to meet the Russian arrival in 1812.
result: Roughly 30 to 70 men guarding the Golden Gate across five decades
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault), compiled from C-A 10, 16, 21, 54

name: Castillo de San Joaquín (Fort Point, San Francisco)
summary: The battery at the Golden Gate narrows, blessed December 1794. Built for 6,491 pesos, partly with mission mule labor. The register's headline series: the fort's serviceable guns never exceeded a handful, and a single Russian outpost at Ross reported more mounted cannon than the whole San Francisco defense.
result: At its documented best (1802): about 5 mounted serviceable guns
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault); build cost C-A 24 Docs 62, 70
notes: The 1793 (2 vs 6) and 1823 (2 vs 3) figures each differ between Savage copies of the same report; both discrepancies are preserved rather than harmonized.

name: Batería de Yerba Buena (San Francisco)
summary: The cove battery east of the presidio, garrisoned in the 1790s by a Catalan Volunteers detail relieved every 8 days. Ordered recomposed with adobe, earth, and fascine in 1799; abandoned by 1800 per the intelligence layer of the borderlands map.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Presidio of Monterey
summary: The capital's presidio and the largest company in the province, with the Real Cuerpo de Artillería headquartered here. Even so, in 1809 its ~85 men were dispersed as mission escorts and herd guards, with only 4 men on the battery.
result: The largest single garrison, comparable to Ross's combined personnel, 100+ miles from the contested ground
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Presidio of Santa Bárbara
summary: Founded 1782 with about 58 men and holding near that strength for decades. In 1797 its artillery inventory recorded 118 cartridges and no artilleryman.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Presidio of San Diego
summary: The first presidio, founded 1769. In September 1783 the whole company held 72 cartridges. Its guns were dismounted in 1793 with nobody able to operate them.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Fort Guijarros (Punta de Guijarros, San Diego)
summary: The harbor battery on Ballast Point, formally the Castillo de San Joaquín de Punta de Guijarros. The province had two forts of that name; this is the San Diego one. In 1798 it mounted 7 six-pounders of which 2 were serviceable; the 1820 census found the bronze guns vent-worn and the carriages rotted.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Presidio of Loreto (Baja California)
summary: The old Baja capital, included for context: its company (47 to 85 men plus a small marine department) was comparable to any Alta California presidio.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Colony Ross (Russian benchmark)
summary: The measuring stick. A single Russian-American Company outpost, founded September 1812 with about 95 Russians and 80 Alaska Native hunters. A 1813 Spanish intelligence report credited it with about 13 mounted cannon; Moraga's 1814 eyewitness reconnaissance counted 8 cannon in two corner towers with embrasures for far more. Either figure matches or exceeds the serviceable artillery of the entire San Francisco defense in the same decade.
result: One Russian fort ≈ the principal Spanish fort, in guns and in men
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault), section 0
notes: Both the Ross figure (a Spanish estimate) and the SF figure (a Spanish self-inventory) are Spanish-sourced, so the comparison is internally consistent. The defensible claim is order-of-magnitude parity, not a precise gun-for-gun ratio.

name: Suscol / Soscol (Mariano G. Vallejo)
summary: About 84,000 acres that General Mariano G. Vallejo bought from Governor Micheltorena in 1843, running from Rancho Petaluma east to the Carquinez Strait and taking in Vallejo, Benicia, and Mare Island. The United States rejected the claim: in United States v. Vallejo (1862) the Supreme Court held that the governor had no authority to sell public land, voiding what would have been the largest grant of the north bay.
sources: Diseño: “Map of Suscol” (Bancroft Land Case Maps) | U.S. land-claim case no. 318 (Vallejo, claimant), Northern District of California | Boundary approximate — claim rejected, no U.S. patent
notes: The circle marks the approximate extent of the claim, not a surveyed boundary; the U.S. never patented Suscol.

name: Mare Island / Isla de la Yegua (Victor Castro)
summary: The island of Mare Island (Isla de la Yegua), about 900 acres, granted to Victor Castro — provisionally by the secretary Jimeno in 1840 and in fee by Governor Alvarado in 1841. Castro sold it to John B. Frisbie and B. R. Simmons; the U.S. Navy bought the island in 1853 for its Pacific shipyard. The grant overlapped Vallejo's Suscol claim and its title was likewise contested.
sources: U.S. land-claim case no. 311 (Mare Island; Bissell, claimant), Northern District of California | Boundary approximate — small contested island grant

name: Echeandía opens partial emancipation
summary: Gov. Echeandía's emancipation program begins: qualified neophytes of the southern missions may leave mission discipline, with individual segregation licenses following (Gil Riela and Andrés Ibarra among the first named). The 1826 San Diego dossier ties the friars' constitutional oath to neophyte emancipation and floats a neophyte pueblo at San Fernando or San Luis Rey.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 27) Doc 127 (the 1826 oath-and-emancipation dossier). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 47) Doc 71 (segregation of Gil Riela, 30 Apr 1826).
notes: The proclamation's own text is not in the vault surveys; its execution is. Standard accounts date the proclamation July 1826.

name: Pre-secularization land census ordered
summary: The Diputación orders every mission to report its lands and boundaries before year's end — the first territorial step toward disentailment. The resulting 1828 'Informes sobre terrenos y ganados' series, with each mission's cattle brand, survives in the State Papers: Missions volumes.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43) Doc 1 (bando, 7 Oct 1827). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Docs 402–412, 418 (the 1828 informes).

name: Echeandía's secularization decree
summary: 'Ley secularizando las Misiones, declarándolas pueblos' — 33 articles converting the missions to pueblos under the 1813 Cortes law, San Gabriel and San Carlos first, extended to all by art. 24. Read to the neophytes at the Monterey-district missions that January; suspended by Gov. Victoria within days, denounced to Mexico, and annulled by the central government in April 1832.
sources: Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 224 (the 33 articles, complete). | St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 29 (the decree). | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 3–5 (promulgation to the neophytes, Jan 1831).
notes: The C-A 49 copy sits after Nov-1831 letters in the volume; the surveys flag the year for verification against Bancroft/Hutchinson.

name: The Mexican secularization law of Aug 17, 1833
summary: The national statute: 'Sobre secularización de las misiones de Alta y Baja California,' converting each mission to a secular parish. The Californian archive's own copy survives in the Superior Government State Papers, with the 26 Nov 1833 colonization companion law that underwrote the Híjar-Padrés colony.
sources: Sup. Govt. St. Pap. (C-A 57) Doc 93, orig. pp. 415–416. | Sup. Govt. St. Pap. (C-A 57) Doc 94 (the 26 Nov 1833 colonization law).

name: Gómez Farías: all missions, four months
summary: The general secularization decree from Mexico: ALL the republic's missions to be secularized within four months. It reached California as Figueroa and the Diputación were already drafting their own, more gradual machinery.
sources: Sup. Govt. St. Pap. (C-A 57) Doc 95.

name: Figueroa's Reglamento Provisional
summary: The instrument that actually dismantled the system: missions partially converted to pueblos; each family head a solar of up to 400 varas and half the livestock; article 18 barring the Indians from alienating their grants; article 22 barring mass slaughter of herds. Enacted through the Diputación's article-by-article debate that July, with same-day instructions to the comisionados — general inventories, dissolution of the monjerío, rancherías of 25 families eligible to form pueblos.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 78, Sav. 253–257 (the printed reglamento). | C-A 53 Doc 79 (Instrucciones para los Comisionados, 12 prevenciones). | Leg. Rec. (C-A 60) Doc 2 (the Diputación debate, Jul 1834). | Leg. Rec. (C-A 59) Doc 31 (the c. 1828–30 'Plan para convertir en pueblos las Misiones', the Diputación blueprint).

name: Alvarado's administrators' reglamento
summary: A ~14-article code for the mission administrators — render accounts, no credit against mission property 'por ningún pretexto,' padrón of neophytes — the government's attempt to police the men it had put over the ex-mission estates. A further mission decree followed on 17 Apr 1839.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., San José (C-A 45) Doc 68 (the reglamento). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 639 (the 17 Apr 1839 decree, sent to Durán).
notes: The standard accounts' 'Jan 17, 1839 regulation' matches neither vault instrument exactly; both are shown.

name: Administrators suppressed, mayordomos created
summary: Alvarado's 1 March 1840 decree suppresses the mission administrators and replaces them with mayordomos under the Visitador's oversight — the government's verdict on six years of administrator rule. Emancipation power was reserved exclusively to the government that October.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Decrees & Despatches (C-A 36) Doc 63, tomo p. 155. | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 646 (16 copies to Durán, 8 Apr 1840). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 596 (emancipation reserved to the government, 23 Oct 1840).

name: Micheltorena returns 12 missions to the friars
summary: The reversal: twelve named missions returned to the padres 'como en tutoría de los Indígenas,' remitting an eighth of their products — after a February order suspending all further alienation of mission lands. The 3 April circular ordering administrators to hand over names ten of them.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 175, Sav. 669–674. | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 1043 (the handover circular, 3 Apr 1843). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 1016 (the Feb 1843 alienation freeze).

name: Pico's sale-and-lease reglamento
summary: The 23-article 'Reglamento para la enajenación y arriendo de las Misiones': sell San Rafael, Dolores, Soledad, San Miguel, and La Purísima; lease the rest for nine years. Chapter 4 declares the neophytes freed and 'no estando obligados á servir á los arrendatarios'; article 20 lets Indians petition for inalienable title to their house and garden plots. Andrés Pico and Juan Manso had been inventorying the missions since May — the commission's object expressly their arrendamiento.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Decrees & Despatches (C-A 36) Doc 107 (verbatim, 23 arts.). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 1225 (the commission's lease mandate, 1 Jul 1845). | C-A 53 Doc 191 (Pico & Manso commissioned, 11 Jul 1845).

name: Mexico orders the sales suspended
summary: The supreme government, learning what the Department 'ha dispuesto' with the missions, orders all alienation proceedings reported and suspended. The sales went ahead anyway.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 181.

name: The Assembly authorizes outright sale
summary: Pico's government, invoking the common defense 'en caso de una invasión extranjera,' authorizes auctioning the missions to pay their creditors, any surplus to each mission's Indian community. The June 1846 deeds of sale cite this decree as their authority.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Decrees & Despatches (C-A 36) Doc 110. | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 160 (the San Buenaventura escritura quoting the 13 Apr decree).

name: The Assembly annuls Pico's sales
summary: With the American conquest underway, the Departmental Assembly annuls the mission sales (art. 1) while continuing the leases (art. 3). The U.S. courts finished the job: the Supreme Court later voided the San Gabriel and San Luis Rey sales.
sources: Unbound Docs. (C-A 63) Doc 479 (verbatim abstract). | U.S. v. Workman (1863) per Caragozian, CSCHS (standard account).

name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
summary: Secularized under the 1834 program; José Joaquín Ortega administered the ex-mission from April 1835. Sold to Santiago Argüello in the last weeks of Mexican rule.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Docs 57–58 (inventory & plano). | Unbound Docs. (C-A 63) Doc 393 (the Argüello sale, 8 Jun 1846). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: An 1847 charge alleged the Argüello bill of sale was ante-dated (C-A 63 Doc 190).

name: Mission San Luis Rey
summary: The richest inventory in the record: $203,787 existencia across the mission and its ranchos (Pala, Santa Margarita, Temécula, San Jacinto). Pío Pico, first a comisionado, administered it to 1840 — removed only under threat of punishment — and its Luiseño residents mounted the most sustained documented resistance to the new order.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 15 (the 1835 general inventory). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 657 (the forced handover order, 23 Jul 1840). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The Cot & Pico sale of 1846 is not in the vault surveys; the July 1846 Marrón handover is.

name: Mission San Juan Capistrano
summary: The earliest secularization — Echeandía's pilot — and in 1841 the first ex-mission formally converted to a pueblo, with a 17-article reglamento and a land repartimiento naming its neófitos libres. Sold in December 1845 for $710.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161 (Pico's consolidated alienation record). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The two vault sale records disagree on the second buyer — 'James McKinley' (C-A 51 Doc 161) vs 'Santiago Machado' (the título, C-A 63 Doc 508c). Both shown; unresolved.

name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel
summary: Handed from Fr. Estenaga to comisionado Nicolás Gutiérrez in November 1834 with 12,980 cattle on its books; by the 1840 inventory the herd had collapsed to 72. Leased under Pico's program — the lease drive began here — and in the vault record assigned to Henry Dalton in February 1846.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 16 (the 1834 handover accounts). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 54 (the 1840 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The Reid & Workman sale of June 1846 is not in the vault surveys as read; the U.S. Supreme Court later voided the San Gabriel sale (standard account).

name: Mission San Fernando Rey
summary: Entrega to comisionado Antonio del Valle in December 1834; a decade later, leased to Andrés Pico and Juan Manso, then sold to Eulogio Célis in June 1846 for $14,000 'para sostener la integridad del Territorio.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 445 (the 1834 entrega). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: Lease figures differ between the two vault records ($1,120 vs $1,125); both shown.

name: Mission San Buenaventura
summary: Among the last secularized: Gov. Chico ordered Fr. Blas Ordaz to hand it to Carlos Carrillo in June 1836 amid the constitutional-oath fight. Sold to its lessee José Arnaz in June 1846 — 'dueño legítimo… para siempre' — followed by an 1846–48 asset-stripping dossier.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 157 (the Chico expediente). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 160 (the deed of sale). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The 1846–48 fraud dossier on the lease is C-A 63 Doc 464.

name: Mission Santa Bárbara
summary: Comisionado Anastacio Carrillo took the richest coastal plant in the 1835 inventory — $113,960 existencia including Rancho Dos Pueblos — with $2,484 in goods distributed to the Indians. Leased in December 1845 to Nicolás Den and Daniel Hill.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 443 (the 1835 inventory). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission Santa Inés
summary: Secularized in the 1836 wave on Chico's order; Fr. Jimeno handed it to José María Covarrubias that August with an existencia of $56,437 — down to $39,284 within six months. Leased in 1845 to Covarrubias himself with Joaquín Carrillo.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 36 (the 1836 inventory). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission La Purísima Concepción
summary: Inventoried under article 15 of Figueroa's reglamento by comisionado Domingo Carrillo, with William Dana as appraiser: existencia $62,088.50 including ranchos Todos Santos and Guadalupe. One of the five missions Pico's reglamento listed for outright sale — bought by John Temple for $10,110 in December 1845.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 439 (the 1834 inventory). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The survey flags the inventory digits as scale-2 reads pending verification.

name: Mission San Luis Obispo
summary: A revolving door of administrators (Trujillo, Moreno, Ayala, Canet, Bonilla); 253 souls in 1834. Erected into a pueblo in July 1844 — its emancipados barred from selling their lands — then sold in December 1845 to Scott, Wilson & McKinley.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The $510 price is the standard account; the vault record gives the buyers, not the price.

name: Mission San Miguel Arcángel
summary: In January 1831 its neophytes refused Echeandía's secularization outright — 'quieren seguir bajo el actual sistema' — and in 1831 asked to remain 'en estado de Comunidad.' Listed for outright sale in Pico's reglamento; the vault holds no sale record.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Doc 3 (the neophytes' refusal, Jan 1831). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 128 (the 1837 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The 1846 Ríos & Reed purchase is the standard account; not found in the vault surveys.

name: Mission San Antonio de Padua
summary: Fr. Pedro Cabot delivered the mission to comisionado Manuel Crespo in November 1834; the 1836 inventory totaled $93,122 across eleven named ranchos, with $13,602 distributed to the Indians and a 'Pueblo de San Antonio' of 557 souls. Offered in 1845, it drew no bidders and was never sold.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 448 (the 1834 entrega). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
summary: Inventoried in August 1835 (~$47,297 — Savage himself noted the figures don't reconcile); 177 souls by 1837. Sold in June 1846 to Feliciano Soberanes, the same encargado instructed in 1840 that 'ningún indígena será forzado á servir á un particular.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 161. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission San Carlos Borromeo (Carmel)
summary: One of the two missions Echeandía's 1831 decree named to go first. By 1839 juez interino Marcelino Escobar held the buildings under a room-by-room inventory, with solares assigned — two to the neófitos Josecillo and Antonio. Its surplus buildings were saleable under the 1845 reglamento; no sale appears in the vault.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Juzgados (C-A 33) Doc 8 (the 1839 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Handed over in May 1835 with a $147,413 existencia including Rancho San Felipe, and a padrón of 63 emancipated Indians holding $5,120 in land. An 1849 retrospective recorded it 'declarada pueblo' a dozen years earlier, its mission houses destroyed for materials.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 14 (the 1835 handover). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission Santa Cruz
summary: Comisionado Ignacio del Valle inventoried ~$84,354 in December 1835. Listed for outright sale in Pico's reglamento; no sale appears in the vault — and in 1849 Hartnell judged that the priest 'has no right at all to sell any real estate or the mission Sta Cruz.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 452 (the 1835 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission Santa Clara de Asís
summary: Administered by the Estradas, then Ignacio Alviso, whose 1840 handover inventory counted 3,847 cattle (down from 5,500 the year before). Its mission houses were barred from sale in 1845; in 1849 the priests leased Santa Clara and San José together to James D. Steinberger for $22,000.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 99 (the 1840 handover). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission San José
summary: Still the great stock estate of the north after secularization — José de Jesús Vallejo's 1840 receipt counted 20,000 cattle and 15,000 sheep — while draining $16,809 to the government. Hartnell's 1840 visita found 589 souls who 'quieren otro administrador.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 143 (Hartnell's San José visita). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The reported 1845/46 sale is disputed between the standard accounts and not in the vault; left open.

name: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Dolores)
summary: Inventoried at $67,227 in July 1835 under comisionados Ignacio del Valle and José Joaquín Estudillo; by the 1841 padrón, 78 souls remained. One of the five listed for outright sale in 1845; no sale record survives in the vault.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 27 (the 1835 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.

name: Mission San Rafael Arcángel
summary: The poorest inventory of the set ($18,474, with Rancho Nicasio at $7,256), but the most direct distribution: 343 Indians received rams, ewes, horses, and mares by name. By Hartnell's 1840 visita they refused a mayordomo altogether — 'no querían ya misión.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 458 (the 1834 inventory). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 149 (Hartnell's San Rafael report). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: The reported $8,000 sale of 1846 is the standard account; no vault record.

name: Mission San Francisco Solano (Sonoma)
summary: Secularized under M. G. Vallejo as comisionado (standard account); the vault's mission-property record names Vallejo, Salvador Vallejo, and mayordomo Antonio Ortega, and shows the mission's stock drawn down for the frontier colony and recruitment in 1835. Its final disposition does not appear in the vault surveys.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 140. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) — year grain.
notes: Excluded (with San Rafael) from the Diputación's c. 1828–30 pueblo plan as too new.

name: The Híjar-Padrés colony lands at San Diego
summary: The brigantine Natalia — the Compañía Cosmopolitana's own ship — reaches San Diego with Director General José María Híjar, Buenaventura Araujo, and 129 colonists, the vanguard of the ~204-person colonization scheme budgeted at 45,206 pesos under the 26 Nov 1833 law. The mission estates were to be its endowment.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Doc 243 (the arrival report, 4 Sep 1834). | St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Docs 51–53, 90–93 (appointment, roster, budget).

name: Figueroa keeps the missions: the contramando
summary: Santa Anna's countermand — carried north 'por extraordinario violento' — orders Figueroa not to hand Híjar the political command; the Diputación's acuerdo goes further: neither the command 'ni los bienes de las Misiones, que son propiedad de los indios.' The colony is stranded, and the principle that the estates belong to the Indians is stated at its plainest.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Official Corr. (C-A 37) Doc 73 (the countermand, leaf-verified). | C-A 37 Doc 78 (the Diputación acuerdo, 22 Oct 1834).

name: Araujo and the armed rising at San Gabriel
summary: In the colony crisis's ugliest episode, ~200 armed Indians briefly seize Fr. Estenaga at San Gabriel; colony officer Buenaventura Araujo is charged with instigating the rising. Ten northern missions are nonetheless ordered to provision the stranded colonists for a year.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 249, 253, 257–260 (the Araujo proceedings).

name: Híjar and Padrés deported on the Loriot
summary: After the Los Angeles plot to depose Figueroa and halt secularization, the colony's leadership is shipped to Mexico: the Loriot's six-article instructions name Híjar, Padrés, Francisco Torres, and Apalátegui among the deportees. Figueroa's manifesto had already given the government's verdict: 'el verdadero y único objeto de su plan es el robo de los bienes de las misiones.' Padrés protested his rights from on board.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 29) Doc 25 (the Loriot instructions). | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (C-A 39) Docs 187–…, and C-A 29 Docs 11–30 (the crisis dossier).

name: Hartnell named Visitador General
summary: William Hartnell is named Visitador of the missions at $2,000 a year — the government's inspector over its own administrators — his salary apportioned mission by mission. His two circuits of 1839–40 produced the most unsparing record of the ex-mission estates that survives.
sources: Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 397 (the appointment). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 434 (the salary apportionment).
notes: He resigned 6 Oct 1840 and ceased functions 7 Nov 1840 (C-A 49 Doc 660; C-A 51 Doc 150).

name: The southern visita: 'los indios son acreedores'
summary: Hartnell's report on the missions from San Diego to San Fernando: the San Dieguito Indians 'son acreedores á la tierra que reclaman'; San Juan Capistrano's community memorial against administrator Argüello arrives 'firmado por José Fermín á nombre de la comunidad'; San Fernando counts 416 souls, its Rancho San Francisco 'taken from them and given to Antonio del Valle.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 151 (the 24 Jun 1839 report).

name: San Rafael: 'no querían ya misión'
summary: On the northern circuit Hartnell finds the San Rafael Indians refusing mayordomo Gregorio Briones and refusing the institution itself — 'no querían ya misión.' His 14 May report to Jimeno Casarín is the keystone document of Indian liberty in the northern ex-missions.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 149 (the San Rafael report).

name: Vallejo arrests the Visitador
summary: At Yerba Buena, M. G. Vallejo intercepts and arrests Hartnell rather than let the inspection reach his Sonoma frontier arrangements — the plainest demonstration of where power over the ex-mission estates actually lay.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 149 (reported with the San Rafael visitation).

name: San José visita: 589 souls, 50 lashes
summary: Hartnell counts 589 souls at Mission San José, records punishments running to 50 lashes — double his own 25-lash cap — and the Indians' verdict: 'quieren otro administrador.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 143.

name: San Diego district: Pico, Temecula, and inventory fraud
summary: The southern return visit: Pico has told the Indians the governor gave him Temecula; Las Flores brings its complaints; and comisionado Carlos Castro's inventory fraud is recorded — the Visitador's file on how the estates were actually being run.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 148 (the 26 Aug 1840 report).

name: San Miguel refuses secularization
summary: Read Echeandía's bando, the San Miguel neophytes answer that 'quieren seguir bajo el actual sistema' — while San Luis Obispo's elect four Indian comisarios de policía under it. The record of divided Indian judgments on emancipation, at the very start.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 3–5 (the promulgation record).
notes: Later (1831) they ask to remain 'en estado de Comunidad.'

name: The southern missions demand the promised land
summary: Neophytes of San Diego, San Juan Capistrano, San Gabriel, and San Luis Rey mobilize to demand the land distribution Echeandía had promised — proclaiming the reformer governor against his replacement. Secularization's first mass Indian politics.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA (C-A 34) Doc 330. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 115–116.

name: 'Somos libres': San Luis Rey refuses to work
summary: Portilla's reports from San Luis Rey: the Luiseños refuse absolutely to return to mission labor — 'somos libres, no queremos volver, no queremos trabajar.' The plainest statement of what emancipation meant to the emancipated.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 156 (Portilla → Figueroa).

name: 'Que no nos pelen las nalgas á azotes'
summary: The San Juan Capistrano neophytes — fewer than 60 still working, the rest fleeing — petition Alvarado against their administrator in their own unsparing words: that they not be flogged raw. Received weeks into Hartnell's visitaduría, it is the Indian-voice document of the administrator era.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 47 (the petition).

name: The Las Flores bargain
summary: Figueroa's oficio records the pueblo de Las Flores — the neophyte pueblo created from San Luis Rey's asistencia — accepting liberty in exchange for subsisting on its own labor. One of the few documented free-Indian pueblos of the secularization.
sources: Unbound Docs. (C-A 63) Doc 15 (transcribing the 29 May 1835 oficio).

name: Temecula and Pala stand armed against the Picos
summary: When the Picos moved on Temecula — Pico telling the Indians the governor had given it to him — the juzgado record shows the rancherías in arms: 'toda la gente está armada.' The Luiseño ranchos defended the land through the juzgado and, when needed, with weapons in hand.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 141 (the juzgado record). | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 20) Doc 226 (the Temecula land conspiracy record: the land 'propiedad de todos').

name: José Cupertino petitions for absolute emancipation
summary: A sixty-year-old Santa Clara man, in service since childhood, petitions for his absolute emancipation — the individual face of the paper freedom the decade had constructed.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Prefecturas y Juzgados (C-A 42) Doc 687.

name: 'Como á hija de la Misión': Feliciana Valdés claims land
summary: An Indian woman petitions for her share of the secularized lands 'como á hija de la Misión' — a daughter's claim on the estate. Hartnell denied it; the file preserves a woman's legal argument for what secularization had promised.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Docs 168–172.

name: Jonatas — Las Olivas
summary: First stop north of mission, at Las Olivas (present-day Los Olivos area).
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 1)

name: Saca — Alamo Pintado Creek
summary: Village of Saca on Alamo Pintado Creek.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 1)

name: Olomosong — Sisquoc River
summary: Probably on the Sisquoc R. near the 120th meridian.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 1: 'After 4 leagues further travel')

name: Geep — South Slope, Sierra Madre
summary: Apparently on the south slope of the Sierra Madre range. After climbing a mountain they came out onto the Cuyama Valley plains. T 10 N, R 28 W.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 1)

name: Talhulimit
summary: Two leagues east of Geep, in the Cuyama Valley.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 1)

name: Lisahua — Salisbury Canyon
summary: Probably in lower Salisbury Canyon. T 9 N, R 26 W.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 2)

name: Camp — Lower Santa Barbara Canyon
summary: In lower Santa Barbara Canyon. T 9 N, R 25 W.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note (cont.))

name: Sgene — Lower Cuyama Valley
summary: Party bore more to the north and found Sgene. T 10 N, R 25 W.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 3)

name: Malapoa — Bitterwater / Santiago Creek
summary: Located by Gifford & Schenck on Bitterwater or Santiago Cr. Identified as Tlamini (Kroeber).
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 4)

name: Sispetis — SE Buena Vista Lake
summary: Considered to be Pohatan Tinliu, at the SE corner of Buena Vista Lake.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 4: Kroeber (1925, pl. 47))

name: Buenasvista — 8 Leagues North
summary: Eight leagues north of Bitterwater/Santiago Cr.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 5)

name: Tejon / El Paso Creek — Foothills
summary: Six leagues from Sispetis to the mouth of Tejon or El Paso Cr. at the edge of the foothills. July 26 reconnaissance explored El Paso, Tejon, and Pastoria creeks.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 6)

name: Tupal — Tejon Ranch on El Paso Creek
summary: Placed doubtfully by Gifford & Schenck at Tejon Ranch on El Paso Cr.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 6)

name: Tacui — Tecuya Creek
summary: Party doubled back west past Grapevine Cr. to Tacui, undoubtedly on Tecuya Cr.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 7)

name: Yagueleme — Kern River / Woilo
summary: Nine leagues north of Tecuya, on the Kern R. Gifford & Schenck identify as Woilo, very close to 9 leagues from Tecuya.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 8)

name: Eastern End of Kern Lake
summary: The eastern end of Kern Lake.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 9)

name: Tashlpj — Pastoria / Grapevine Creek
summary: Cook thinks more likely Pastoria on Grapevine Cr. rather than Tejon Cr., since the party arrived at Castaic at the head of Grapevine Cr. on August 7.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 10)

name: Castaic — Head of Grapevine Creek
summary: Party arrived August 7. Beginning the crossing south.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions

name: Antelope Valley
summary: Crossed into Antelope Valley.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 11)

name: San Gabriel Mountains Crossing
summary: Party crossed the mountains and went southwest. Several villages of Serrano Indians seen.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 12)

name: Mission San Gabriel
summary: Arrival at San Gabriel Mission.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 12)

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Departure, late September 1806. Fr. Pedro Muñoz accompanying as chaplain.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions

name: San Benito River Camp
summary: 1½ leagues from the mission, on the San Benito R.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 13: 'not on Pacheco Cr., as stated by Cutter')

name: San Luis Ranch — Pacheco Pass
summary: Camp approximately at San Luis Ranch, where Highway 152 crosses San Luis Cr.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 14)

name: Santa Rita Camp
summary: 15 to 20 mi east of San Luis Gonzaga. Near Salt Slough or Paso Slough, 5–6 mi west of the main San Joaquin.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 15: 'The sloughs and channels of the San Joaquin are difficult to locate with precision on a modern map')

name: Camp on the San Joaquin
summary: On the San Joaquin R. T 8 S, R 11 E.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 16: villages effaced so thoroughly that modern informants gave no indication they ever existed)

name: Bear Creek
summary: Rather than Mariposa Cr. Approximately 3 leagues south of the Merced R.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 18: 'Cutter thinks this was Bear Cr... I see no reason to disagree')

name: Merced River — West of Livingston
summary: Party which went north reached the Merced R. somewhere west of Livingston, probably at T 6 S, R 11 E.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 19)

name: Dry Creek
summary: Undoubtedly Dry Cr. 'The description is valid even today.'
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 21)

name: Tuolumne River Area
summary: Villages seen on the Tuolumne but were deserted. Oak forest environment.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook notes 20, 24: Taulames village between the Tuolumne and Stanislaus)

name: Stanislaus River — Near Modesto
summary: Remnants of the oak forest can still be seen, extending from the junction with the San Joaquin eastward. Both sides of the river.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 22: 'if it continued in a northwesterly direction from near Modesto')

name: Upper Stanislaus — Knights Ferry Area
summary: Six leagues upstream. Vicinity of Ripon, Riverbank, or Knights Ferry. Limestone bluffs, precipitous. The best guess is the vicinity of Knights Ferry.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 23)

name: Calaveras River
summary: First stream (Rio de ... Franciscos) identified as the Calaveras.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 25: 'There is little reason to disagree')

name: Cosumnes River — Northernmost Point
summary: Second stream identified as the Cosumnes. Linguistic border between Miwok and Maidu. The diarist fails to mention the Mokelumne.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 25: northernmost extent of the expedition)

name: Cosumnes River — Turn South
summary: Party turns south, staying close to the eastern edge of the valley along the Sierra foothills.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions

name: Stanislaus / Tuolumne Area (return)
summary: Passing back through the Stanislaus and Tuolumne country.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions

name: Chowchilla / Mariposa Creek
summary: Santo Domingo identified as Mariposa Cr.; Tecolote as the Chowchilla (Cutter).
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 26)

name: Fresno River (Santa Ana)
summary: The Santa Ana was the Fresno R.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 27)

name: San Joaquin at Pizcache
summary: Pizcache on the San Joaquin, listed in the appendix. Moraga probably halted approximately north of Fresno, below Le Grand. Distinct absence of permanent Indian settlements on seasonal streams.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 27)

name: Pitkachi Village Area
summary: Pitkachi 'held the south side of the San Joaquin, living at Kohou, near Herndon or Sycamore; at Weshiu, on a slough; and at Gewachu, still farther downstream.' Village was in the mountains or at least the foothills.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 28: Gayton / Kroeber disagree on exact location)

name: Kings River — Near Sanger
summary: Kings R. was reached near Sanger or Centerville.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 31)

name: Kaweah Delta — Visalia / Telame
summary: 28th day: scouts reached the great oak forest along the Kaweah delta at or above Visalia. 29th day (Oct. 19): main party arrived. The large village of 600 souls — Telame (the Telamni). 22 persons baptized.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 33: 'The water evidently was very low — somewhat unusual for this region, even in October')

name: Tule River — Near Porterville
summary: After a winding course for two days, the party camped on the Tule R. near the foothills, probably not far from Porterville.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 36)

name: Deer Creek
summary: Probably Deer Cr.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 37)

name: White River
summary: Probably White R.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 38)

name: Poso Creek
summary: No distances given, but from the description the most likely stream is Poso Cr.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 39)

name: Kern River — Above Bakersfield
summary: The Kern R., probably some miles above Bakersfield. A 'long trip' downstream brought them into the slough country south of Bakersfield.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 40)

name: Kern River — Downstream / Slough Country
summary: South of Bakersfield. Moraga did not get within sight of Buena Vista Lake, to the west.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook notes 40–41)

name: Grapevine Canyon
summary: Zalvidea had left an account of the villages in this area from his Aug. 1806 expedition.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 41)

name: Tejon Pass
summary: On the last three days the party left the valley by way of Grapevine Canyon, over Tejon Pass.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 42: 'Cutter says the Santa Susanna Range')

name: Mission San Fernando
summary: Arrival at San Fernando Mission. End of the 1806 expedition.
sources: Muñoz/Zalvidea diaries via Cook, Colonial Expeditions (Cook note 42)
